She wants to know where the bathroom is.

To report a statement: il dit que + indicative.
To report a question: il demande si / où / quand / pourquoi / ce que.
To report an order: il dit de + infinitive.
To change pronouns and possessives when reporting (je → il, mon → son).

Friday, 30 April, evening. The grandmother and Radu have arrived in Lyon after thirty hours on the coach. Now they’re having dinner at Madame Bernard’s, with Hélène, Ioana and Julien. The grandmother only speaks Romanian, so Ioana translates.
Welcome to Lyon, madame! Ioana, ask her if the journey wasn’t too hard.
(after translating) She says the journey was long, but that the driver was very nice. His name was Costel and he sang all the time.
And she slept for twenty hours out of thirty. I ate sarmale during the other ten.
Ioana, tell her I’m very happy to meet her. And ask her what she thinks of Lyon.
She says she’s happy too. She says Lyon is very beautiful, but there are too many cars. And she’s asking why French people eat so late.
Ha ha! Tell her we eat late because we talk a lot first.
She answers that it’s the same in Romania, but that in Romania people eat AND talk at the same time.
Ioana, ask her if she wants to see your dress tomorrow. And tell her I’ve learnt a new sentence in Romanian.
She says yes to the dress. And she’s asking what your sentence is. She says she hopes it isn’t one of Radu’s.
(in Romanian, slowly) Vă mulțumesc că ați venit de atât de departe.
(moved) She’s not saying anything… She’s crying. She says it’s the most beautiful sentence she’s ever heard from a Frenchman.
Ioana, tell her too that tomorrow I’d like her to come with me to the bench in Croix-Rousse. The one where I used to wait for Henri.
She’s asking who Henri is. Shall I tell her? It’ll take an hour…
Tell her. We have all the time in the world. And tell her the dessert is Sophie’s tart, the best in Lyon.
(an hour later) She says it’s the most beautiful story she’s ever heard. And she says Sophie’s tart is good… but hers is better.

“Kel dee”: que + elle merge into a single sound. Likewise “qu’il” = “keel”.
“Duh-mãd-lwee”: imperative + pronoun, joined with a hyphen, stress on “lui”.
“Ẽ-ter-pret”: nasal in at the start. Careful: “interprète” = spoken interpreter, “traducteur” = written translator.
“Gar roo-tyair”: the coach station. The train station is simply “la gare”.
1. Reporting a statement: il dit que
When the reporting verb is in the PRESENT (il dit, elle répond, il explique), the tense of the verb does NOT change. Only the pronouns and possessives change, as in English:
Elle dit que son voyage était long.
She says her journey was long.
“Que” is COMPULSORY in French (“Elle dit qu’elle est fatiguée”), although in English “that” can be left out. And it’s repeated in each clause: “Elle dit que c’est long, mais que c’est beau.”
Il demande si tu as faim.
« Où est la salle de bains ? »
Elle demande où est la salle de bains.
She’s asking where the bathroom is.
Elle demande pourquoi vous mangez tard.
She’s asking why you eat late.
Il demande ce que tu veux.
Il demande ce qui se passe.
No “est-ce que” in a reported question! “Qu’est-ce que” becomes “ce que”, “qu’est-ce qui” becomes “ce qui”, and yes/no questions take “si”.
3. Reporting an order: dire de + infinitive
“Don’t worry!” → She says not to worry.
“Tell her!” → She asks us to tell her.
You can also use the subjunctive: “Elle veut que vous mangiez.” But “dire de + infinitive” is simpler and very common.

In mixed families, someone is always translating. Useful expressions for that role:

Some Romanian words have no exact French equivalent: “dor”, “a pofti”, “musafir”. The French have theirs too: “flâner” (to wander about aimlessly), “dépaysement” (the feeling of being far from home).

On Saturday 1 May, Ioana had a hairdresser’s appointment for a trial, and Julien was rehearsing with Théo, the little pianist. So it was Radu who went with his grandmother to Croix-Rousse.

Hélène was already waiting for them on the bench, in front of the chemist’s that used to be Lucette’s café. Madame Bernard was sitting next to her, with Victor on her lap. The weather was lovely. The market on the boulevard smelt of strawberries and warm bread.
The grandmother sat down between the two Frenchwomen. Radu remained standing, a little nervous. He knew he was going to have to translate. And he knew it wouldn’t be easy.
“Ask her how she met her husband,” Hélène began.

Radu translated. The grandmother smiled. Radu listened for a long time, then explained: “She says his name was Ion, that he was the best dancer in the village, and that he asked her to dance at a wedding, in 1965. She says she refused three times, so that he’d understand she wasn’t easy to win over.”

The two Frenchwomen laughed. “And the fourth time?” asked Madame Bernard. Radu translated. The grandmother answered, laughing too. “She says the fourth time, he didn’t ask her. He just took her by the hand. And she danced with him for fifty years.”

Then Hélène told her own story: the café, the Thursdays, the waltz, Henri who had left for Algeria and never come back. Madame Bernard told hers: the port of Marseille, the chocolate ice cream, the fifty years of marriage. Radu translated everything, sentence by sentence, searching for the words.
When they had finished, the grandmother was silent for a long moment. Then she said a single word in Romanian. Radu opened his mouth to translate… and closed it again.

“She says ‘dor’,” answered Radu. “But… it can’t be translated. It’s a Romanian word. It’s when you miss someone, but not only that. It’s a sweet pain. It hurts, but you wouldn’t want it to stop, because it’s all that’s left of the person.”

Hélène looked at the chemist’s, and she saw the café. She looked at the bench, and she saw a young man composing a waltz. “Dor,” she repeated softly. “I think I understand. It’s what I felt for sixty years, without knowing the word.”
Madame Bernard nodded. “Me too. For five years.” The grandmother took the hand of one, then the hand of the other. She didn’t need a translator for that.
Radu moved away discreetly. His eyes were wet, and he didn’t want his grandmothers to see. On the boulevard, he noticed that everyone was buying little bunches of white flowers.
He asked a stallholder what they were. She explained that it was lily of the valley. In France, on 1 May, people give lily of the valley to those they love, to bring them luck all year.

Radu bought three bunches. When he came back to the bench and gave them to the three ladies, Hélène asked him who had taught him this tradition. “Nobody,” answered Radu, blushing. “I saw it, and I understood. Like the word dor.”
The grandmother asked what the flowers meant. When Radu explained, she opened her bag and took out two little objects: two red and white strings, with a little metal clover. Mărțișoare.

Radu translated: “She says that in Romania, on 1 March, people give these for spring and for luck. She says she brought them from Iași for the people she would like to love. She’s asking if you’d be willing to wear them.”

Hélène pinned hers to her coat straight away. “Tell her I’ll wear it on Monday, at the wedding.” Madame Bernard wanted to attach hers to Victor’s collar, but Victor protested so loudly that everyone laughed, even the people at the market.

Before leaving, Hélène asked Radu to tell his grandmother that she wanted them to sit together on Monday. The grandmother answered that she would sit next to her, of course. But that she would dance a lot more than her.

That evening, telling his sister about the day, he said he had been an interpreter for three hours, that he was exhausted, and that it had been the best job of his life. In two days’ time, it would be the wedding.

During the coach journey, Radu sends messages to his sister. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions.
Thursday, 8 a.m. We’re off! Granny says she’s brought three kilos of sarmale. She’s asking if you have enough room in your fridge.
Thursday, 3 p.m. Hungary. The driver is called Costel. He sings songs by Gică Petrescu. Granny sings with him. The whole coach is singing. Help.
Thursday, 11 p.m. Austria. Granny is asleep. A lady asks me what I’m doing in France. I tell her my sister is getting married. She gives me some biscuits for you.
Friday, 7 a.m. Germany. Granny wakes up and asks where we are. I tell her we’re in Germany. She says the fields are very tidy.
Friday, 12 noon. Switzerland. Granny wants to know why the mountains here are higher than ours. I don’t know what to answer.
Friday, 2 p.m. Last message before Lyon. Granny says to tell you she’s very happy. And that she wants Julien to come and pick us up. Not you. Julien.
